newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians hold national unity dialogue.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians hold national unity dialogue.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Thursday chaired a meeting of Islamist and secular Palestinian factions in the West Bank in the first national dialogue in five years, organisers said.

The meeting which brought together senior leaders of groups that support Israeli-PLO peace moves and opponents came one day after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government gave the green light to build a new neighbourhood for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem, threatening Israeli-PLO peace moves.
Palestinians said the participants hoped to agree on a document that would become the reference for Israeli-PLO talks on a permanent peace agreement, due to resume next month.
But at the end of the conference, participants said there was still disagreement over U.N. Security Council resolutions 242 and 338 which serve as the basis for the current Middle East peace process.
The resolutions call for the trading of occupied Arab land for peace and say all states in the area have a right to live within secure and recognised borders.
Participants said a final communique stressed "the right of the Palestinians to defend their rights in Jerusalem and in Palestinian lands against Israeli settlement policy".
"The main result of the meeting was a show of Palestinian unity in the face of Israeli hegemony," said Abdel-Aziz Shaheen, Palestinian minister of supplies.

Abdel Rahim Maluh of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) said the participants had agreed to form a committee that would meet periodically to follow up on the dialogue begun at the conference.
"This committee will include representatives of the Palestinian Authority and the Palestinian factions," he told Reuters.
The last time Palestinians held a national dialogue was in December 1992 in Tunis after Israel deported more than 400 Islamist activists to south Lebanon.

Palestinians said that representatives of the Islamic Hamas group, the Damascus-based PFLP and the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP), and Arafat's Fatah movement were among several factions took part in the talks. The Islamic Jihad was absent.
Relations between PLO and leftist and Islamic groups soured after Arafat signed a self-rule deal with Israel in 1993.
Ties plunged further over the Palestinian Authority's repeated crackdowns on militant Palestinian organisations following attacks against Israelis.
"Our unity is a matter of life or death, especially under the present and most serious stage we live in," Palestinian Legislative Council speaker Ahmed Korei said in a speech at the meeting.
